title: Molecular surveillance of Bartonella species, Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses in wild small mammals and their associated chigger mites in South Korea
authors: Kim B, Lee YJ, Woo HM, Choi JW, Choi I, Kang YM, Kwak D, Seo MG.
abstract: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens. Molecular surveillance incorporating both small mammals and their associated ectoparasites can provide information on pathogen detection at the wildlife-ectoparasite interface. In this study, 1,444 wild small mammals and 12,869 associated chigger mites, analyzed as 680 host-associated pools, were collected from 17 sites in South Korea between 2022 and 2025. Samples were examined for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses using PCR- and RT-PCR-based methods, followed by sequence and phylogenetic analyses. The predominant small-mammal species, Apodemus agrarius, accounted for 84.9% of captured small mammals. DNA related to Bartonella schoenbuchensis was detected in 473 of 680 chigger mite pools (69.6%), whereas DNA related to Bartonella bacilliformis, Bartonella henselae, and Bartonella taylorii was detected in three of 1,444 small-mammal liver samples (0.2%) for each taxon. DNA of Coxiella burnetii was detected in 51 of 1,444 liver samples (3.5%), all collected during the autumn 2024 survey. Orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 37 small mammals (2.6%), predominantly in A. agrarius (35/37, 94.6%), with the remaining two detections in Crocidura spp. (2/37, 5.4%), and in three chigger mite pools (0.4%). To our knowledge, these findings provide the first molecular evidence of DNA related to B. schoenbuchensis in host-associated chigger mite pools and document previously unreported DNA related to B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in wild small-mammal liver samples in South Korea. The results provide descriptive baseline data for wildlife-based molecular surveillance; they do not establish seasonal patterns, individual-mite infection prevalence, or vector competence.

title: Virome characterization of plateau wetlands-collected rodents in western Guizhou Province, China
authors: Zeng X, Tang X, Zhou J, Zhou J, Gu T, Zhao S, Liu C, Hu Y, Li S.
abstract: Rodents carry a diverse range of infectious microorganisms and may serve as potential sources of novel infections for both livestock and humans. The complex ecological network involving humans, migratory birds, and rodents in the Caohai Wetland provides a conducive environment for viral recombination. Continuous virological surveillance of rodent populations is essential for enhancing our understanding of their viral diversity and potential ecological consequences. Although significant progress has been made in sequencing technologies, systematic studies on the viral composition carried by rodents in the wetlands of the Guizhou Plateau remain limited. In our study, viral metatranscriptomes and RT-PCR analyses were performed on the brains, livers, spleens, lungs, kidneys, and intestines of 113 rodents collected from the Caohai Wetland. A total of 144 known and putative viruses were identified in Apodemus chevrieri and Niviventer confucianus, including members of the families Coronaviridae and Hepeviridae, as well as several novel species of Picobirnaviridae and Nodaviridae. These findings substantially advance current understanding of the rodent-associated viral community in the Caohai Wetland on the Guizhou Plateau. The results provide a scientific basis for the evaluation and monitoring of existing and emerging viral threats and establish a broader virological foundation for the prevention and control of potential spillover events associated with rodent-borne infectious diseases.IMPORTANCERodents harbor a diverse array of infectious microorganisms and serve as potential reservoirs for emerging zoonotic pathogens affecting both livestock and humans. Through unbiased RNA sequencing and RT-PCR assays, we identified 144 known and putative viruses in indigenous rodent populations sampled from the Weining Caohai Wetland. These results significantly broaden the current characterization of the rodent-associated virome in the Caohai Wetland and provide critical insights into the host tropism of these viral agents. Moreover, our study establishes a robust, empirically grounded viral baseline, thereby strengthening the foundation for proactive surveillance and evidence-informed prevention of zoonotic spillover events.

title: Interspecific social contacts spread gut microbiota in wild rodent communities
authors: Raulo A, Hanski E, Lamberth C, Firth JA, Knowles SC.
abstract:
Background: The mammalian gut microbiota influences a wide array of host phenotypes and varies substantially among individuals. Among conspecifics, microbiota composition is strongly shaped by microbial transmission through social interactions, yet the extent to which such transmission also occurs across species boundaries remains poorly understood. Here, we combine high-resolution tracking data collected over more than 10 months with gut microbiota profiling to examine social associations, space use, and microbiota similarity among individuals of three sympatric rodent species - wood mice (Apodemus sylvaticus), yellow-necked mice (A. flavicollis) and bank voles (Myodes glareolus), in two woodlands. By integrating multi-species social networks and spatial overlap with individual microbiota data, we test how both conspecific and interspecific interactions shape gut microbiota composition.

Results: At both study sites, social associations strongly predicted microbiota similarity among conspecific individuals, whereas spatial proximity consistently predicted microbiota similarity among interspecific pairs. In addition, social associations between mice of different species predicted microbiota similarity, although this effect was weaker than that observed within species and was asymmetric, with evidence for stronger microbial transmission from wood mice to yellow-necked mice than vice versa. By focusing on species-indicative bacterial taxa, we further show that wood mice with more social connections to yellow-necked mice harboured a greater richness of gut bacteria typical of yellow-necked mice.

Conclusions: Together, these results demonstrate that individual-level social behaviour can influence gut microbial transmission across species boundaries, particularly among closely related species with overlapping ecological niches. Interspecific social interactions may therefore represent an underappreciated pathway for the acquisition of novel gut symbionts in multi-species communities.

title: Wild wood mouse gut microbiota are influenced by captivity and cross-fostering
authors: Bancroft RE, Wolf SE, Hall J, Sweeny A, Pedersen AB.
abstract:
Background Wild and laboratory animals harbour profoundly different gut microbiota, but how microbiomes shift between these states, and the relative roles of captivity, microbial history, and host identity in shaping that shift, remain unclear. Here, we developed a unique wood mouse ( Apodemus sylvaticus ) system comprising free-living mice (Wild: As ), a wild-derived colony maintained in captivity for over a decade (Wild-like: As ), and a second colony that we generated from the Wild-like: As mice by caesarean rederivation and cross-fostering to laboratory Mus musculus (Lab-like: As ). We compared these three Apodemus cohorts with conventional laboratory Mus musculus (Lab: Mm ) to ask how microbial diversity, community composition, and functional potential vary across a spectrum of wild-to-laboratory conditions.

Results We found that alpha diversity varied substantially among cohorts but showed no consistent wild-to-laboratory trend: Shannon diversity was higher in Lab: Mm and Lab-like: As than in Wild: As and Wild-like: As mice, whereas phylogenetic diversity was similarly high in both the Wild: As and Lab:Mm groups. Community composition more closely reflected cohort histories. Despite over a decade in captivity, Wild-like: As mice remained most similar to Wild: As conspecifics, whereas Lab-like: As mice shifted strongly away from Wild-like: As and toward, but remained distinct from, Lab: Mm mice. The clearest wild-to-laboratory pattern emerged in microbiome consistency: core ASVs (present in ≥90% of individuals) increased from 9 in Wild: As to 46 in Wild-like: As , 72 in Lab-like: As , and 138 in Lab: Mm mice. Predicted functional potential revealed a further distinction between taxonomic and functional patterns: Wild: As and Wild-like: As microbiomes did not differ significantly, whereas Lab-like: As shifted toward the Lab: Mm state despite remaining taxonomically distinct.

Conclusions Together, these results show that laboratory-associated microbiomes do not emerge through simple loss of wild microbial diversity, but through broader reorganisation of community composition, consistency, and predicted functional potential reflecting microbial history and host context. The persistent Wild-like and Lab-like microbiome states within Apodemus provide a powerful experimental system for future timely work testing how microbiome history influences host physiology, resilience, and responses to environmental challenges.

title: Habitat-mediated reassembly of rodent assemblages along an urban–suburban–rural gradient
authors: Ren Z, Zhang C, Feng Y, Chen J, Xia T, Niu H, Zhang H.
abstract:
Abstract

Urbanization profoundly alters habitats and biological communities; however, its impacts on rodent assemblages and functional traits across varying habitat types remain inadequately understood. We surveyed rodents across 81 subplots encompassing woodland, farmland, and residential habitats along an urban-suburban-rural gradient in Wuhan, a rapidly urbanizing megacity of central China. We collected data on species composition, external morphology, organ traits, and local environmental covariates, analyzing them via multispecies count models, beta-diversity partitioning, community-weighted mean trait decomposition, ordination, path analysis, and nested cross-validation. In 9,720 trap-nights, we captured 246 individuals representing six species across four genera. Capture success increased from urban to rural sites and was significantly higher in farmland and woodland than in residential areas. Rodent assemblage composition varied significantly with urbanization, habitat type, and their interaction, with habitat explaining a substantially greater proportion of the variation. Residential assemblages were characterized by larger body-sized Rattus spp., whereas farmland and woodland were dominated by the smaller Apodemus agrarius and Niviventer confucianus , respectively. Among-site variation in community-level body size was primarily driven by species turnover and shifts in dominance, whereas organ traits exhibited high intraspecific heterogeneity that was not consistently explained by the measured environmental variables. Furthermore, human activity intensity was significantly associated with assemblage composition. These findings suggest that urbanization shapes rodent functional composition predominantly through habitat-mediated species turnover and dominance shifts, rather than through uniform intraspecific responses. This study underscores the necessity of habitat-specific rodent monitoring and management strategies in rapidly urbanizing landscapes.

title: Meteorological factors and haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome incidence in ten provinces of China, 2005–2020: a two-stage, age- stratified distributed lag non-linear analysis
authors: Wang F, Tai M, Ke M, Liu Y, Duan Y, Chen T, Tian Z.
abstract:
Abstract

Background Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a rodent-borne zoonosis with its largest burden in China. Meteorological conditions influence transmission, but age- and endemic-type-specific associations remain unclear, and most multi-region studies lack population denominators. Methods We analysed 132,313 age-stratified HFRS cases reported during 2005–2020 in ten Chinese provinces, grouped by reservoir-host seasonality into Apodemus-type, Mixed-type and Rattus-type regions. Population denominators came from three censuses and revised intercensal series; monthly meteorological exposures came from quality-controlled national stations. Within each province and age stratum (0–19, 20–59, ≥ 60 years), we fitted quasi-Poisson distributed lag non-linear models (lag 0–6 months) with a log person-month offset and mutual exposure adjustment, pooling reduced curves by endemic type and stratum. Curve robustness was assessed using best linear unbiased predictions and a 2,000-draw bootstrap; null results were bounded by minimum detectable relative risks; provincial covariates were examined in meta-regressions. Results The 20–59-year stratum contributed 75.8% of cases (annual incidence 1.70 per 100,000, versus 0.33 at 0–19 and 1.57 at ≥ 60 years). In Apodemus-type provinces, precipitation showed an inverted-U association peaking at 175.9 mm (relative risk (RR) 2.73, 95% CI 1.44–5.18), strongest at ages 20–59 (190.6 mm, RR 3.08, 1.14–8.37) and robust to leave-one-province-out analysis (95th-percentile RR 1.44–3.52). Temperature peaked near 8.7°C (RR 1.44, 0.34–6.01). Humidity associations were weak on average but diverged across climate zones (dry-promoting in Shaanxi versus humid-promoting in Shandong), producing near-flat pooled curves (I² up to 72.8%). The two Rattus-type provinces showed opposite temperature-curve directions (heat-promoting in subtropical Yunnan, cold-promoting in temperate Hebei) and are therefore reported per province. Age stratification eliminated Apodemus-type precipitation heterogeneity in the 0–19 and ≥ 60 strata (I² = 0%). Provincial ageing rate explained temperature-curve heterogeneity (P = 0.004; I² reduced from 60.0% to 40.2%). Detectability bounds indicated adequate power for moderate precipitation effects at working ages, but not for temperature extremes in sparse strata. Conclusions Meteorological–HFRS associations are structured by reservoir-host endemic type, concentrated in the working-age population, and modified by population ageing. Age-stratified designs with population denominators are essential for unbiased multi-region synthesis.

title: Insights into Mycoplasma spp. genetic diversity through a long-term study in bank voles (Clethrionomys glareolus) in the Mazury Lake District in Poland
authors: Alsarraf M, Dwużnik-Szarek D, Wężyk D, Alsarraf M, Tołkacz K, Romanek W, Grzybek M, Górska J, Krupińska M, Goll A, Freitas FM, Behnke-Borowczyk J, Behnke JM, Bajer A.
abstract:
Abstract

Hemotrophic mycoplasmas (hemoplasmas) are Gram-negative, uncultivable bacteria that parasitize red blood cells of diverse vertebrates. Rodent-associated hemoplasmas with zoonotic potential have been reported, highlighting the need to study these pathogens in wild rodent populations. We investigated the prevalence, abundance, and genetic diversity of Mycoplasma spp. across three geographically separated populations of bank voles, Clethrionomys glareolus (n = 1514), sampled over 23 years. Additional positive samples were obtained from Apodemus flavicollis , A. sylvaticus , and A. agrarius . Prevalence was assessed using microscopic examination and molecular identification based on the 16S rRNA gene (595 bp). Infection abundance was quantified by counting infected erythrocytes in 200 microscopic fields. Genetic diversity and species delineation were evaluated using phylogenetic analyses and Minimum Spanning Network approaches. Overall prevalence of Mycoplasma spp. was 69.4%, with a mean abundance of 12.6 ± 0.69 infected RBCs per 200 fields. Phylogenetic analyses revealed eight previously undescribed Mycoplasma species comprising 16 haplotypes. These findings provide new insights into the prevalence, abundance, diversity, and host associations of Mycoplasma spp. in free-living rodents, demonstrating long-term infection stability and the influence of ecological and demographic factors. This study represents the first molecular investigation of rodent hemoplasmas in Poland.

title: Experience-dependent shifts in behavioural decision-making following repeated captures in a wild mammal
abstract: Live trapping is central to behavioural ecology, yet whether post-capture behaviour reflects consistent among-individual differences and how it is modified by repeated captures remain poorly understood. Here, we repeatedly captured wild individuals of the rodent Apodemus mystacinus and temporarily held them in a standardised wooden experimental box. We then allowed them to voluntarily exit the box near the capture location and continuously recorded their behaviour for 5 minutes. Using multilevel, multivariate and continuous-time multi-state models, we characterise the sequence of behavioural states from confinement to escape. We also test whether capture experience reorganises individual behavioural trajectories and whether individual characteristics, such as body mass and sex, mediate behavioural transitions across capture-recapture events. We show that there is among-individual variation in the measured post-capture behaviours and that repeated captures reorganise the structure and sequential organisation of behavioural responses after individuals exit a trap. Importantly, we also show that recapture experience and body mass are associated with an increased tendency towards rapid escape. In contrast, we find that sex has no detectable effects. Our findings highlight that behaviours expressed immediately after trap release do not represent individuals' undisturbed ecological baseline, but instead experience-dependent responses shaped by individuals' cumulative history of interactions with their environment.

title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis in adrenoleukodystrophy: a new piece in the puzzle?
authors: Torreni L, Schlüter A, Marti S, Ruiz M, Vélez-Santamaria V, Rodríguez-Palmero A, Artuch A, Guilera C, Arias A, Mochel F, Aguilera-Albesa S, Cantarin V, Casasnovas C, Artuch R, Köhler W, Pujol A, Fourcade S.
abstract: ABSTRACT X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) is the most common monogenic disorder affecting brain white matter, presenting a broad clinical spectrum from slowly progressive adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN) to rapidly advancing cerebral demyelination. Factors influencing the variable disease expressivity remain poorly understood. We conducted shotgun metagenomic profiling of fecal samples from X-ALD patients and integrated these data with targeted plasma metabolomic analyses of amino acids and key metabolic intermediates. We identified distinct microbiome-associated metabolic signatures across X-ALD phenotypes. Notably, Bacteroides cellulosilyticus and Helicobacter apodemus abundance were significantly altered in AMN compared with childhood CALD patients. In parallel, X-ALD patients exhibited evidence of microbial metabolic remodeling characterized by altered amino acid metabolism, reduced folate biosynthetic potential, and enrichment of stress-adaptive pathways, including redox-associated functions, glyoxylate shunt activity, lipid A modification, lipopolysaccharide assembly, biofilm adhesin biosynthesis, and curli fiber production. Consistent with these microbial changes, plasma levels of branched-chain amino acids and methionine, as well as serum folate concentrations, were significantly reduced. Importantly, methionine levels showed an inverse correlation with neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentrations in patients with cerebral disease. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized link between gut microbial metabolic capacity and systemic metabolic alterations in X-ALD. Our results reinforce previous evidence implicating methionine metabolism in disease severity. Collectively, these data support a modulatory role of the microbiota–gut–brain axis in neuroinflammatory and mitochondrial-related processes underlying X-ALD progression and highlight new opportunities for biomarker development and microbiome-informed therapeutic interventions.
